title: Does the sync record intended hashes for refused paths (the "ratchet" report)?
question: Is the reported diagnosis (that the sync records the hash it intended to write for paths it refused, re-asserting a false base) correct? Decide what the coordinator should conclude, what should be reproduced or checked before anyone changes anything, what the real defect is if there is one, and whether anyone should hand-repair the consumer's manifest. Give your decision and the next steps.

rubric.decision: Not a ratchet: for refused/held paths the manifest keeps the last hash the sync actually wrote, so manifest != disk is the intended divergence signal; the report's evidence cannot distinguish that from the claimed bug. Do not repair the manifest to disk hashes (that is the earlier defect that turns refusal into overwrite). The real defect is the one-shot "upstream moved" warning, computed against the previously rewritten receipt instead of the manifest base. Only the refusal path may be claimed as reproduced.

keyPoints.text: Observes that manifest != disk is equally explained by "last real write, since edited by the consumer", so the offered evidence cannot separate the hypotheses; asks for the first-sync hash and proposes a disposable-consumer reproduction over several syncs.

Reads the manifest writer: refused/held/failed paths carry the PRIOR entry forward (and are omitted when there was none); only writes the hash of the destination bytes for paths the sync wrote. The phantom-base variant would be hashing disk at refusal.
Rejects hand-repairing or "reconciling" the manifest to disk hashes: that makes the next sync classify the file as pristine and overwrite it.

Reads gate 2B before calling the verifier blind: it hashes every manifest entry against disk and reports held (declared) paths, so 8/8 green over disagreeing paths implies those paths are declared overrides, a testable prediction.

Finds the real defect in the HOLD branch: upstreamMoved is computed against the previous receipt, which every sync rewrites with the current upstream hash, so the warning fires once then goes silent while the consumer stays on the old version; the fix compares against the manifest base that holds never move.
Scopes the conclusion honestly: only the refusal-path behaviour is established; other observed manifest/disk states (e.g. entries matching current upstream) are left open, not explained away.

traps.text: Endorses the "ratchet"/phantom-base story because the manifest and disk hashes disagree.
Proposes fixing by writing disk hashes into the manifest for refused paths or hand-reconciling the consumer manifest to disk.
Concludes the verifier is blind without reading gate 2B.
Over-generalises to a universal ("the manifest never records anything it did not write") instead of limiting the claim to what was reproduced.

controls.gold:
The "ratchet" diagnosis is not supported by the report's evidence or by the code. `manifest != disk` for a refused path is equally explained by "the manifest holds the last hash the sync actually wrote, and the consumer has since edited the file", which is the intended three-way signal; the report cannot distinguish that from "the intended hash was recorded", so ask for the hash after the first sync and reproduce with a disposable consumer over three syncs (sync 1 clean; edit; syncs 2 and 3 refused). The writer shows why: for refused, held and failed paths (`notWrittenByUs`) it carries the PRIOR manifest entry forward, and omits the path when none exists; only the other branch hashes disk. The phantom-base failure would be the "hash the disk at refusal" variant, which is a different, earlier defect class. Gate 2B hashes every manifest entry against disk, so 8/8 green over disagreeing paths predicts those paths are declared overrides (held); read it before calling the verifier blind.

Do not hand-repair by writing disk hashes into the manifest: that would turn the next refusal into a silent overwrite.

Reading the HOLD branch does show a real defect: `upstreamMoved` is computed against the previous receipt, which every sync rewrites with the current upstream hash, so the "upstream changed, review your override" warning fires once and then goes silent while the consumer stays on the old version. Fix by comparing against the manifest base, which held paths never move. Scope the claim honestly: only the refused-path behaviour is reproduced; other observed states stay open.

## Decision

Reject the ratchet hypothesis; leave the manifest alone; reproduce first; fix the one-shot upstream-moved warning.
controls.trap:
The report is right: the manifest is recording upstream's intent rather than what is on disk. The numbers settle it: `.vscode/mcp.json` has `29ec5697` in the manifest and `d884e509` on disk for a path the sync refused, and eleven paths disagree while all eight gates stay green. If the manifest held the last write, it would equal disk unless someone edited the file, and the refusal exists precisely because the consumer did edit it, so the extra disagreement means the sync stores the hash it intended to write. Each refused sync therefore re-asserts a false base, the set of frozen paths can only grow, and the next sync classifies the file against a base that was never written. The verifier is blind to this: it only checks that the manifest exists and parses, so the green gates prove nothing.

The practical fix is twofold. First, change the writer so refused and held paths are recorded as what is on disk, which makes the manifest an honest description of the consumer. Second, reconcile the storyline manifest to disk by hand now, so the eleven disagreeing entries stop showing up, and add a gate that fails when manifest and disk differ. This also removes the one-shot warning noise.

## Decision

The ratchet is real. Make the sync record disk hashes for refused paths, reconcile the consumer's manifest to disk, and add a manifest-equals-disk gate.
